title: How to Thrive as a Single Christian
excerpt: Singleness is not a waiting room. The church has often treated it that way, and single people have often believed it. Both were wrong.
body:
Somewhere along the way the church started talking about singleness as a problem to be solved, a temporary condition you endure until the real life starts. I have done this myself, from a pulpit, without meaning to, by the way I prayed for single people and the way I never quite let them lead anything that married couples led. We made a whole stage of life sound like a holding pattern. Then we wondered why single Christians felt like they were sitting in the back of the room.

Paul did not think this way. He was single, and he wrote that he wished more people were free to live as he did (1 Corinthians 7:7). Jesus was single. The two people the New Testament holds up most are not married. That should at least slow us down before we treat marriage as the goal and singleness as the detour.

## Stop living provisionally

The deepest trap of singleness is the provisional life. You do not buy the good furniture because you might move when you marry. You do not put down roots in a church because you might meet someone in another city. You hold your whole life loosely, waiting for the second half to begin, and meanwhile the only half you have been given slips by unlived.

The correction is not denial. It is commitment. Plant something. Buy the dishes. Join the church and serve in it like you will be there in ten years, because you might. A life held provisionally is a life half-refused, and God did not give you a provisional life. He gave you this one.

## Build a household that is not romantic

We have shrunk the word family until it means only spouse and children. The Bible's word for the people you do life with is bigger than that. The early church called each other brother and sister and meant it, sharing meals and money and burdens.

Singleness goes wrong when it becomes isolation. It goes well when it becomes a different shape of belonging. Make a standing dinner. Take a family in your church and become a fixture in their kids' lives. Travel with friends. Be the one who shows up. Loneliness is not cured by marriage and it is not cured by being alone with your thoughts. It is cured by being woven into people who count on you.

## Use the freedom you actually have

Paul's argument for singleness was not that it hurts less. It was that it frees you for undivided devotion (1 Corinthians 7:32-35). A married person's time and money and attention are rightly divided. Yours are not, and that is not a deprivation. It is a capacity.

You can say yes to the mission trip. You can give more than the median because you do not have a mortgage built for two incomes and three children. You can sit with the dying friend until two in the morning. The freedom is real, and the question is whether you will spend it on the kingdom or on yourself. Most of us spend it on ourselves. That is the actual temptation of singleness, and almost no one names it.

## Let the longing be honest

None of this means the desire for marriage is wrong, and I am not going to tell you to pray it away. You can want a thing God has not given and still live fully. The two are not in competition. Hannah wept in the temple and was not rebuked for it (1 Samuel 1). The longing is allowed to be real. What it is not allowed to do is run your life from the shadows, turning every gathering into a search and every friendship into a disappointment that it was not more.

Name the longing to God plainly. Then set it down and go live. The longing will still be there tomorrow. So will the life you are refusing to live while you wait.

## This week

Do one thing that a provisional life would not do. Buy something for your home you have been deferring until marriage. Or commit to a role in your church that assumes you will be there in three years. Pick the one that exposes how much you have been waiting, and do it on purpose.

Singleness is not less. It was the soil the church grew in. The question is not when your real life begins. It already has.

title: How to Date With Wisdom
excerpt: Most dating advice is either too casual or too anxious. There is a third way, slower than the culture and warmer than the rulebook.
body:
I have watched two kinds of Christian dating fail, and they fail in opposite directions. One treats it like shopping, swiping through people the way you scroll a menu, always wondering if a better option is one screen away. The other treats it like defusing a bomb, so heavy with rules and red flags and spiritual interrogation that no actual human can survive the first three coffees. Both miss the point. Dating is not a marketplace and it is not a doctrinal exam. It is how you find out, honestly and over time, whether you and another person could build a life that serves God together.

## Date toward marriage, not toward feelings

The culture dates toward feelings. You go out to see if the spark is there, and when it fades, as feeling always does, you assume the relationship is over. This produces a string of intense beginnings and no endings that mean anything.

Wisdom dates toward a question, not a feeling. The question is simple: could I become more like Christ alongside this person, and could they become more like Christ alongside me? Attraction matters and I am not pretending it does not. But attraction is the doorway, not the house. Plenty of people you are attracted to would make your faith smaller. Date toward who you would become, not toward how you feel in the first month.

## Watch character before chemistry

Chemistry tells you almost nothing about whether someone will be faithful when faithfulness is expensive. Character tells you everything. So watch the things chemistry distracts you from. How do they treat the server, the waiter, the person who can do nothing for them? What do they do when they are wrong? Do they apologize cleanly, or do they manage you into thinking it was your fault?

The Bible's word for the thing you are looking for is steadfastness, the quality of someone who keeps their word when keeping it costs them. You cannot see it in a good week. You see it in how they handle disappointment, traffic, their family, and being told no. Slow down enough to see those things before you decide.

## Bring it into the light

Dating in secret is dating in danger. The relationships that go badly wrong, morally and otherwise, are almost always the ones nobody else can see. So let people see it. Introduce them to your friends early, not because you are sure, but because you want people who love you watching while your judgment is compromised by hope.

Ask a married couple you trust to know the person. Ask them to tell you the truth, even the truth you do not want. Proverbs says there is safety in many counselors (Proverbs 11:14), and it does not add an exception for romance. Your friends can see what you cannot, because they are not falling for anyone.

## Guard the body and the timeline

I am not going to give you a rulebook for physical boundaries, because rulebooks get gamed and the point is not the rule. The point is that physical intimacy bonds two people faster than knowledge can keep up, and a body convinced it is married will lie to a mind that is still deciding. Go slower than your body wants. The slowness is not prudishness. It is keeping your judgment unbribed.

And watch the timeline. Endless dating with no movement toward decision is its own kind of dishonesty, a way of taking the comfort of a relationship without the risk of committing to one. If after a reasonable time you cannot say yes, it is more loving to say no than to keep someone in a holding pattern your indecision built.

## This week

Name one thing about the person you are dating, or the kind of person you want to date, that has nothing to do with how they make you feel. Watch for it this week. If you are not dating anyone, ask one married couple you respect what they actually look for in a spouse. Their answer will teach you more than any list.

Dating with wisdom is slower than the culture and warmer than the rulebook. It is not about finding a flawless person. It is about telling the truth, in the light, with people watching, toward a life you could build together.

title: How to Know If You Should Marry Someone
excerpt: Nobody arrives at this decision with certainty. But there is a difference between healthy uncertainty and the doubt you are training yourself to ignore.
body:
People come to me before a wedding looking for permission, and what they usually want is for me to confirm a decision they have already made. Sometimes I can. Sometimes I sit there listening and realize they are asking me to silence a doubt they should be listening to instead. So let me say the thing first: nobody marries with certainty. If you are waiting to feel one hundred percent sure, you will wait forever, because marriage is a covenant made by two people who cannot see the future. The question is not whether you are certain. The question is whether your uncertainty is the ordinary kind or the warning kind.

## The questions worth more than feelings

Strip away the feeling for a moment and ask the structural questions, because these are the load-bearing walls of a marriage.

Do you respect them? Not just love, respect. Would you want to become more like this person? Marriage shapes you toward your spouse over the decades, and if you do not respect who they are, you are agreeing to be slowly shaped toward someone you do not admire.

Do they make your faith bigger or smaller? Not whether they are religious in the same way, but whether being near them draws you toward God or quietly away. Paul's instruction to marry in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39) is not snobbery. It is the recognition that you become one flesh, and one flesh cannot be split down the middle on the thing that matters most.

Can you fight well? Every marriage fights. The question is whether you can disagree and repair, or whether conflict turns into contempt and silence. Watch how you handle your worst moments together, not your best. The worst moments are the marriage you are actually signing up for.

## Listen to the people who love you

Here is a hard truth. The people who love you and are not in love can often see what you cannot. If your closest friends and your family are uneasy, and they are people of wisdom and not just protectiveness, do not dismiss them because your heart has already voted. Ask them directly: what do you see that I do not? Then sit in the discomfort of their answer.

I have rarely seen a marriage where everyone who loved the couple had serious reservations turn out to be a marriage they were glad they fought for. The voices of wise people around you are a gift God gives precisely because love makes you a poor judge of the person you love.

## The difference between cold feet and a real warning

Cold feet is fear of commitment itself, the weight of forever, the vertigo of choosing one life and closing others. That fear is normal and it is not a reason to stop. A real warning is different. A real warning is a specific, recurring thing you keep explaining away. The temper you keep excusing. The dishonesty you keep reframing as a quirk. The way they treat you when no one is watching that you keep telling yourself will change after the wedding.

It will not change after the wedding. Whatever you are tolerating now, you are agreeing to tolerate for life, often in a heavier dose. Marriage does not reform people. It magnifies what is already there. So ask honestly: is my hesitation about the size of the step, or about this specific person? Those are different feet getting cold.

## What you are actually promising

Marriage is not a reward for finding the right person. It is a promise to become the right person, to one specific human, through everything. The vow is not I will stay while you make me happy. It is I will stay (Ecclesiastes 4:9-12). So the final question is not only whether they are worth marrying. It is whether you are ready to be the kind of person who keeps a covenant when it costs.

## This week

Write down the one doubt you have been refusing to look at. Then ask one wise person who loves you, and is not afraid of you, to tell you the truth about your relationship. Let them finish before you defend anything.

You will not get certainty. You can get clarity. The difference between them is the difference between a feeling and a decision made with your eyes open.

title: How to Handle a Breakup
excerpt: A breakup is a small death, and we keep telling people to get over it like it was a head cold. Grief that is rushed does not heal. It hides.
body:
We do not have good language for the end of a relationship that was not a marriage. There was no funeral, no casserole brigade, no time off work. People expect you to be fine in a week because, technically, nothing legal happened. But something did happen. A future you had started to imagine is gone, and futures, even imagined ones, take real grief to bury. I have sat with people leveled by a breakup who were embarrassed to be leveled, because the culture told them it was minor. It was not minor. Let me say that plainly first.

## Grieve it like the loss it is

The worst thing you can do is rush. We are uncomfortable with grief, so we cover it, with a new relationship, with frantic activity, with the performance of being totally fine. But grief you bury alive does not die. It waits, and it comes out sideways months later in a way you do not connect to its source.

So let yourself mourn. Tell God the truth about it. The Psalms are full of people saying out loud how much they hurt, and God did not edit those prayers out of the Bible (Psalm 34:18). You are allowed to be sad about a real loss. The sadness is not weakness or lack of faith. It is the cost of having loved someone, and that cost is honorable.

## Go quiet before you go searching

The instinct after a breakup is to fill the hole immediately. A rebound, a dating app downloaded the same night, a new person to make the old one jealous. Resist it. A wound you build a new relationship on top of does not heal. It just becomes the foundation of something built crooked.

Give yourself a real stretch of being alone with God and a few good friends before you start looking again. Not as punishment, but because you cannot choose well from a place of panic, and grief is a kind of panic. The person you would pick to stop the pain is rarely the person you would pick clear-eyed. Wait until you are choosing from fullness, not from a hole.

## Resist the urge to rewrite the story

When a relationship ends, the mind does one of two cruel things. It either makes the other person a villain, so you can be angry instead of sad, or it makes them perfect, so you can ache over the one who got away. Both are lies that make grief easier in the short run and slower in the long run.

Tell the truth instead. They were a real person, with real good and real failures, and so were you. You contributed to how it ended; almost everyone does. Owning your part is not self-punishment. It is how you learn something instead of repeating it. The person who refuses to see their own hand in every ending will keep finding the same ending in every relationship.

## Let it form you

There is a kind of person who comes out of a breakup more bitter, more guarded, more convinced that love is a con. And there is a kind who comes out softer, wiser, more able to love well. The difference is not how badly they were hurt. It is what they did with the hurt, whether they let it close them or let it teach them.

God does not waste pain. Romans says he works even this toward good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and that is not a slogan to skip past the hurt. It is a promise to be tested on the far side of it. Ask him what this is meant to form in you. Sometimes the answer is patience. Sometimes it is the slow death of an idol you had made out of being chosen. Let the loss do its work.

## This week

Stop performing fine. Tell one trusted person the actual truth of how you are doing, and then tell God the same, out loud, without cleaning it up. Delete the dating app for two weeks, not forever, just long enough to grieve before you search.

A breakup is a small death. Buried honestly, it heals. Rushed or denied, it festers. Give it the grief it asks for, and it will give you back to yourself, more whole than before.

title: How to Build Deep Friendships as an Adult
excerpt: Most adults are lonely and would never say so. Friendship does not happen to grown-ups by accident anymore. You have to build it on purpose.
body:
When you were young, friendship was nearly free. You were thrown together, in classrooms and dorms and on teams, in the same place at the same time week after week, and depth happened without anyone deciding it would. Then you grew up, and the shared space disappeared. Now everyone is busy, scattered across the city, drowning in obligations, and the friendships that used to grow on their own require something they never required before. They require intention. Most adults never make the switch, which is why so many of us are quietly lonely and would die before admitting it.

## Admit that proximity is gone

The first thing to accept is that the old conditions are not coming back. You will not stumble into a best friend at the office the way you did in college, not usually, because adult life does not provide the repeated, unhurried proximity that depth needs. If you wait for friendship to happen to you, you will wait alone.

So you have to manufacture the proximity that life no longer hands you. This sounds unromantic, scheduling friendship like a dentist appointment, and it feels that way at first. But every deep adult friendship I have is one I or the other person chose to keep showing up for, on purpose, when it would have been easier not to. The spontaneity is a lie we tell ourselves. The showing up is the real thing.

## Choose a few and go deep

The culture pushes width, a wide network of acquaintances, hundreds of contacts, dozens of people you wave to. Scripture pushes depth. Jesus had crowds, but he had twelve, and inside the twelve he had three. He did not try to be close to everyone. Neither should you.

Pick a small number of people and invest disproportionately in them. Depth requires repetition, the same people over a long time, which means you cannot do it with everyone. Choosing a few is not a failure to love widely. It is the only way anyone has ever loved deeply. A friend who sticks closer than a brother (Proverbs 18:24) is not a friend you found by networking. It is one you made by staying.

## Go first, and go past the surface

Adult friendship stalls at the weather. Two men can know each other for a decade and never get past sports and work, because someone has to go first into the real conversation and nobody wants to be the one who makes it weird. Be the one who makes it weird. Ask the question under the question. Say the true thing about how you are actually doing.

Friendship deepens at the speed of disclosure. When you risk telling someone something real, you give them permission to do the same, and the relationship can move. Stay safe, and it stays shallow forever. The vulnerability has to go first, and it usually has to be you, because everyone is waiting for someone else to make it safe.

## Build it around something

The strongest adult friendships are usually built around a shared thing, not just a shared feeling. Men especially tend to bond shoulder to shoulder, working on a project, rather than face to face, talking about feelings. So give the friendship a structure. A standing breakfast. A project. A small group that actually meets. A workout. Serving together at church.

The structure carries the friendship through the dry weeks when neither of you feels like it, and the dry weeks are exactly when most adult friendships quietly die. Two believers who confess sin to each other and pray (James 5:16) have a structure stronger than mood, and mood is not strong enough to sustain anything over years.

## This week

Text one person you would like to be closer to and propose something specific and recurring, a monthly breakfast, a weekly walk, not a vague let us hang out sometime. Then, the next time someone asks how you are, tell the truth instead of saying fine. Go first.

Friendship will not happen to you anymore. You are an adult, and the free version expired. But the built version, chosen and tended on purpose, is deeper than anything proximity ever gave you for free.

title: How to Set Healthy Boundaries With In-Laws
excerpt: Leave and cleave is not a suggestion. A marriage needs a fence around it, and building that fence kindly is one of the first jobs of a new family.
body:
The Bible's first instruction about marriage is not about love or sex. It is about leaving. A man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife (Genesis 2:24). That word leave is the part everyone skips, and skipping it has wrecked more young marriages than infidelity. You cannot fully cleave to a spouse while you are still primarily attached to your parents, and many of us try, and then wonder why the marriage feels crowded.

Let me be clear about what this is not. It is not cutting off your parents, dishonoring them, or treating them as the enemy. The same Bible that says leave also says honor your father and mother (Exodus 20:12), and that command never expires. The work is holding both at once: a marriage with a clear fence around it, and parents who are still honored and loved on the other side of the fence.

## The marriage is the new center

When you marry, the unit of allegiance changes. Your spouse is now your primary family, and your parents become extended family, deeply loved but no longer at the center. This shift is the whole game, and it has to be real, not just theoretical.

Practically, it means your spouse hears things before your mother does. It means when there is a conflict between your spouse and your parent, you do not automatically side with the parent you have known longer. It means decisions about your money, your kids, your holidays, and your home are made by the two of you, and then communicated, not submitted for approval. A young couple that still runs every decision past a parent has not finished leaving, and the marriage will pay for it.

## Each spouse manages their own parents

Here is the rule that prevents the most damage: you handle your parents, and your spouse handles theirs. When a boundary needs to be set with your mother, you set it, not your spouse. Nothing breeds resentment faster than making your husband or wife be the one to confront your difficult parent while you stay safely out of it.

This takes courage, because confronting your own parent is harder than confronting your in-law. But it is right, and it protects your spouse from being cast as the villain who took you away. When your parents see that you are the one holding the line, the line holds, and your marriage is not the scapegoat.

## Set the fence with kindness, not heat

Boundaries set in anger feel like attacks, and they provoke the war they were meant to prevent. Boundaries set calmly, in advance, before the holiday blowup, are received as information rather than rejection. So have the conversation when nothing is on fire. We love having you, and we have decided that on Christmas morning it will just be us and the kids, and we would love you to come at noon. Warm, clear, not negotiable, not cruel.

Expect pushback, especially the first time, especially if the pattern has been the opposite for years. People who have had access to all of you do not lose it gracefully. Hold the line without escalating. You can be both kind and immovable; in fact, the kindness is what makes the immovability bearable.

## Present a united front

Whatever you decide, decide it together and deliver it together, so that no in-law can split you. The moment a parent senses that one of you disagrees with the boundary, they will work that seam, and the marriage will crack along it. Disagree in private, all you need to. In front of the families, you are one.

This is the practical meaning of one flesh. It does not mean you never differ. It means the seam between you is not available to anyone outside the marriage as a place to push. Guard that seam, and the in-law relationships, far from suffering, usually get healthier, because clear fences make good neighbors of everyone.

## This week

If there is a boundary you have been avoiding with your own parents, name it to your spouse first, agree on the wording together, and then you, not your spouse, have the conversation. Set it warm. Set it once. Then hold it.

Leave and cleave is not rejection of your parents. It is the building of a home with walls, so that the new family God made when you married has a place of its own to grow.

title: How to Be Content When You Long to Be Married
excerpt: Contentment is not pretending you do not want the thing. It is the harder, truer work of being whole while you wait, with the longing still alive.
body:
There is a cruel piece of advice floating around the church that goes: stop wanting marriage and God will give it to you. As if desire were the obstacle, as if contentment meant successfully lying to yourself about what you want. I do not believe it, and I do not think the Bible teaches it. Paul says he learned to be content in any situation (Philippians 4:11-12), and the word he uses does not mean he stopped wanting things. It means he found a stability underneath his wanting, a floor that held whether the want was satisfied or not. That is what we are after. Not the death of the longing. A floor beneath it.

## Contentment is learned, not summoned

Notice that Paul says he learned contentment. It was not a temperament he was born with or a switch he flipped. It was a skill built over years, through plenty and hunger, abundance and need. This should relieve you, because it means your present discontent is not a verdict on your faith. It means you are in the middle of the learning, not failing the test.

So stop expecting to feel content as if it should arrive whole. Treat it as a practice, something you build by repetition, the way you build a muscle. The repetition is what the rest of this is about.

## Refuse the lie that marriage completes you

Under a lot of the ache is a false belief, half-cultural and half-romantic, that a spouse would fix what feels broken or empty in you. Marriage does not do that. I have done plenty of weddings and plenty of counseling, and I can tell you the lonely single person who believes marriage will cure their loneliness becomes the lonely married person who is shocked it did not.

Marriage does not complete you. It exposes you. It takes the cracks you already have and presses on them. The person who is whole in Christ before marriage brings wholeness into it; the person who is desperate for marriage to fix them brings the desperation in, and it gets worse, not better, with an audience. Your completeness has to be sourced somewhere marriage cannot touch (Colossians 2:10), or marriage will disappoint you exactly as much as singleness does.

## Let the longing drive you to God, not away from people

There are two ways the longing for marriage can go. It can curdle into bitterness, self-pity, and withdrawal, where every wedding is a wound and every couple a reproach, and you slowly pull back from the very community that could hold you. Or it can become a kind of prayer, an honest ache you keep bringing to God, that drives you deeper into him and further into people rather than out of them.

The difference is whether you let the longing isolate you. Hannah longed for a child so deeply she could not eat, and she took the longing into the presence of God and poured it out (1 Samuel 1:15). She did not pretend she was fine, and she did not let it pull her into a hole. She wept it out before the Lord and then went back to her life. Do that. Bring it to God raw, then go love the people in front of you.

## Build the full life now

Contentment grows in a full life, not an empty one waiting to be filled. So fill it. Deep friendships, meaningful work, real service, a household of people who count on you, a faith you are actually building rather than pausing. A person whose life is rich in these things can hold the longing for marriage without being ruled by it. A person whose life is thin and reserved, waiting for a spouse to give it meaning, will be ruled by the longing because there is nothing else in the room.

This is not a consolation prize. It is the life God has actually given you, and it is enough to be lived fully, longing and all.

## This week

Name the longing honestly to God, out loud, the way Hannah did, without cleaning it up. Then do one thing that builds the fullness of the life you already have, and would build it whether or not you ever marry. Invest in a friendship, take a role, serve someone.

Contentment is not the absence of wanting. It is a floor beneath the wanting that does not move. You can want marriage with your whole heart and still stand on that floor. That is not pretending. That is being whole while you wait.

title: How to Handle Loneliness
excerpt: Loneliness is not a character flaw and it is not always solved by being around people. It is a signal, and the question is what you do with it.
body:
The first thing to say about loneliness is that it is not a sin and it is not a weakness. Even Jesus, in the garden, asked his friends to stay near and watch with him, and grieved that they could not (Matthew 26:38-40). The God who made us said before anything had gone wrong, before sin, that it is not good for the human to be alone (Genesis 2:18). So if you are lonely, you are not malfunctioning. You are responding correctly to a real lack. The ache is doing its job. The question is what you do with the signal, because loneliness handled badly becomes a prison, and loneliness handled well becomes a door.

## Tell the difference between solitude and isolation

These are not the same thing, and confusing them keeps people stuck. Solitude is being alone and at peace, the chosen quiet where you meet God and yourself. Isolation is being alone and aching, cut off from the connection you were made for. Jesus sought solitude constantly, withdrawing to lonely places to pray (Luke 5:16). He did not seek isolation.

The trap is that isolation disguises itself as solitude. You tell yourself you are fine being alone, you are introverted, you do not need people, and meanwhile you are slowly withering. Be honest about which one you are in. If your aloneness restores you, it is solitude, keep it. If it drains and dims you, it is isolation, and it needs a different answer.

## Resist the instinct to withdraw

Loneliness has a cruel logic. It tells you to pull back further, that reaching out is too risky, that people would not want you anyway, that it is safer to stay in. Every one of those messages deepens the very thing it claims to protect you from. Loneliness, left alone, recruits you into your own imprisonment.

So the first move against it is almost always to push against the instinct. Go to the thing you do not feel like going to. Send the text you are afraid to send. Show up to the gathering when every cell in you wants to stay home. You will not feel like it; that is what loneliness does, it kills the appetite for the cure. Act against the feeling, not from it. Connection is built by the people who show up before they feel like it.

## Move toward others, not just toward being filled

There is a kind of lonely person who goes to people only to be filled, and stays empty, because they arrive as a need rather than a presence. Counterintuitively, one of the surest exits from loneliness is to stop hunting for someone to meet your need and start meeting someone else's. Serve. Notice the other lonely person in the room and go to them. Visit the widow, the shut-in, the new person nobody is talking to.

This is not a trick and it is not denial of your own need. It is the strange economy Jesus described, that you find your life by giving it away (Mark 8:35). The lonely person who pours out is met in the pouring, while the lonely person who only seeks to be filled often stays empty no matter how full the room.

## Let it drive you to God

Underneath every human loneliness is a deeper ache that no person was ever meant to fully fill. We keep asking spouses and friends and crowds to be God for us, and they cannot, and we call the resulting disappointment loneliness. Some of your loneliness is for people, and you should pursue people. Some of it is for God, and only he fits that hollow (Psalm 73:25-26).

This does not make human connection optional; God himself said it was not good to be alone, and then made us for each other. But it does mean a friend who expects another human to cure all of it will exhaust that human and stay lonely. Bring the deepest part of the ache to the only One who can hold it, and bring the human-shaped part of it to actual humans. Most of us mix these up, asking people for what only God gives and asking God for what he intends to give us through people.

## This week

Do the one thing your loneliness is telling you not to do. Reach out to a specific person, by name, this week. Then find someone lonelier than you and go toward them. The signal is real. The answer is a door, not a deeper room.

title: How to Find a Mentor
excerpt: Most people wait to be chosen by a mentor and never are. Mentoring is not a program you get assigned to. It is a relationship you go and build.
body:
Almost everyone wants a mentor and almost no one has one, and the gap between those two facts is mostly a misunderstanding about how mentoring works. People imagine a wise older person will notice their potential, take them under a wing, and pour into them over coffee for years, all without ever being asked. That happens about as often as winning a raffle. The real thing is less magical and more available: you find someone further down the road than you, you go to them, and you ask. The reason you do not have a mentor is usually that you have not asked anyone to be one.

## Know what you are actually looking for

Before you ask, get clear on what you want, because mentoring is not one thing. Sometimes you need a guide for a specific skill, someone who has done the job you are learning. Sometimes you need a model for character, an older saint whose life you want yours to resemble. Sometimes you just need someone older and wiser to ask the hard questions.

Paul tells Titus that the older are to teach the younger (Titus 2:3-5), which assumes the structure already exists in the church if we will use it. So look around your actual life, your church, your work, your family, and identify someone two or three steps ahead of you in the direction you want to grow. Not a celebrity. Someone you can have lunch with. The best mentors are usually near, not famous.

## Ask small, not for forever

Here is where most people sabotage themselves. They walk up to a busy, accomplished person and ask, will you mentor me, which is an enormous, vague, open-ended request that most wise people will gently decline because they do not know what they are agreeing to. Instead, ask small and specific. Could I buy you coffee and ask you three questions about how you handled X? That is a thirty-minute commitment, not a lifetime, and almost anyone will say yes.

Then, if the coffee goes well, ask for another one. Mentoring relationships are almost never established by a formal agreement. They grow by accumulation, one good conversation leading to the next, until one day you realize this person has become a mentor without either of you ever using the word. Start with the small ask. Let it build.

## Be the kind of person worth investing in

Mentors invest in the teachable, and they can spot the unteachable in one conversation. If you ask for advice and then defend yourself against all of it, you will not get a second meeting. If you ask for time and then do not act on what you were given, the mentor learns that pouring into you is pouring into a sieve. The proverb is blunt: the wise listen and increase in learning (Proverbs 1:5).

So come humble, come prepared, and come ready to do something with what you receive. Bring real questions, not flattery. Follow up to say what you did with the advice. The mentor who sees that their words actually moved you will open the door wider every time, because everyone wants to invest in someone who grows.

## Honor their time and have more than one

A mentor is giving you the scarcest thing they have, which is time they will not get back. Honor it. Be on time, come ready, do not ramble, and do not turn every meeting into unloading your problems. Make it easy to help you. The easier you are to mentor, the longer the mentoring lasts.

And do not pin all your growth on one person. No single human can be your guide for skill and character and faith and career all at once, and expecting that of one mentor will exhaust them and limit you. Build a small set: someone for your work, someone for your walk with God, someone for your marriage. A wise life is shaped by an abundance of counselors (Proverbs 15:22), not by one overworked hero.

## This week

Name one person two or three steps ahead of you in something that matters. Send them a short message this week asking for one coffee and one specific thing you want to learn from them. Keep the ask small. Then show up prepared, listen more than you talk, and act on what you hear.

Nobody is coming to choose you. The mentor you want is probably one honest, specific ask away, waiting for someone humble enough to come and ask.

title: How to Have a Hard Conversation
excerpt: The conversation you keep avoiding is usually the one that would heal the thing. Avoidance is not peace. It is just slower damage.
body:
There is a conversation you are avoiding right now. You know the one. The thing you need to say to your spouse, your friend, your boss, your parent, that you keep not saying because saying it feels dangerous and not saying it feels safe. Here is the hard truth I have had to learn over and over in fifteen years of ministry: the not saying is not safe. Avoidance does not prevent the damage. It just spreads it out over a longer time, lets it grow in the dark, and turns a hard conversation now into a much harder one later, or a quiet death of the relationship that never gets a chance to heal. Jesus did not say blessed are the conflict-avoiders. He said blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and peacemaking is active, not the absence of trouble.

## Go directly, and go alone first

When someone has wronged you, Jesus is specific about the order of operations. Go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone (Matthew 18:15). Alone first. Not to the group chat, not to your other friends, not to everyone except the actual person. We reverse this constantly. We tell everyone but the one who could fix it, which is not addressing the problem, it is just spreading it while looking like we care.

Going directly is harder and far kinder. It gives the person a chance to respond, to explain, to repent, that they never get when you talk around them instead of to them. So before you have the hard conversation in your head with everyone else, have the real one with the person who is actually in it.

## Aim for restoration, not for winning

Before you open your mouth, get your goal straight, because it will leak into every word. If your goal is to win, to be proven right, to make them feel as bad as they made you feel, the conversation will become a battle and you will probably get the fight you came for. If your goal is to restore, to understand and be understood and make the relationship right, you will speak differently.

The aim that Scripture sets is restoration, gently (Galatians 6:1), not victory. This is not weakness. It is harder than fighting, because it means staying soft toward someone who has hurt you. But a conversation aimed at restoration can heal things a conversation aimed at winning will only deepen. Decide your goal before you decide your words.

## Say the true thing kindly, and own your part

Two failures wreck hard conversations. One is honesty without love, the truth delivered like a weapon, accurate and cruel. The other is love without honesty, so much softening and hedging that the actual point never lands and nothing changes. The target is truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), both at once: the real thing said, and said with care.

Use plain words. Speak for yourself, what you saw, what it did to you, rather than narrating their motives, which you cannot actually see. And own your part early. There is almost always a part. Going in with a confession of your own contribution, before you name theirs, disarms the defensiveness that would otherwise eat the whole conversation. The log in your own eye comes first (Matthew 7:5), and naming it first is not just righteous, it is wise.

## Listen like you might be missing something

A hard conversation is not a speech you deliver. It is an exchange, and if you have already scripted their lines and your rebuttals, you are not having a conversation, you are staging a performance with a hostage. Go in genuinely open to learning that you saw it wrong, or partly wrong, because you often have.

Be quick to hear and slow to speak (James 1:19). Ask what you are missing. Let them finish without loading your reply while they talk. People can feel the difference between being heard and being waited out, and almost nothing softens a hard conversation faster than the other person realizing you are actually listening rather than just reloading.

## This week

Name the conversation you have been avoiding, and the person it belongs to. Go to that person directly, this week, alone first. Before you speak, decide that your goal is to restore, not to win, and start by owning your part.

The conversation you dread is usually the one that would heal the thing. Avoidance feels like peace and is only delay. Go and have it, gently, and in the open.

title: How to Forgive Someone Who Has Not Apologized
excerpt: Waiting for an apology that may never come hands the offender control of your healing. Forgiveness is something you can do without their permission.
body:
The hardest forgiveness is the kind no one asks you for. When someone wrongs you and then apologizes, forgiveness is still costly but it has a path. When someone wrongs you and never acknowledges it, never says sorry, maybe does not even think they did anything, you are left holding the whole weight alone, and every instinct says you are entitled to hold it until they make it right. I understand that instinct. I have nursed it. But waiting for an apology that may never come puts the offender in charge of your freedom, and that is a strange prison to choose, the one where the person who hurt you also keeps the key.

## Forgiveness is something you can do alone

Here is the freeing thing, and it took me years to believe it. Forgiveness does not require the other person's participation. It is, at its root, a decision you make before God to release a debt, to stop demanding the payment you are owed (Colossians 3:13). The offender does not have to be present, repentant, or even alive for you to forgive them. You are not waiting on them. You never were.

This is why Jesus could forgive from the cross people who were actively mocking him and had offered no apology. Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34). They had not asked. He did it anyway, because forgiveness is a posture of the heart toward the offender, not a transaction that requires their signature. You can begin it today, with no cooperation from anyone.

## What forgiveness is not

Let me clear away the things people confuse with forgiveness, because the confusion makes them refuse it. Forgiveness is not saying it did not matter; it mattered, which is exactly why it needs forgiving. It is not forgetting; you may remember it the rest of your life. It is not the absence of consequences; you can forgive a person and still not hand them your trust or your front door key. And it is not necessarily reconciliation. Reconciliation takes two people and a repaired trust; forgiveness takes one.

This matters enormously for the unrepentant offender. You can fully forgive someone and still keep a healthy distance from them, still refuse to pretend nothing happened, still decline to reenter a situation that harmed you. Forgiving the person who never apologized does not mean letting them hurt you again. It means releasing your claim on revenge while keeping your wisdom about safety.

## Why you cannot afford to hold it

When you refuse to forgive, you imagine you are punishing the offender, but they are usually living their life untroubled while the poison sits in you. Bitterness does not hurt the person it is aimed at. It hurts the person it lives in. Hebrews calls it a root of bitterness that springs up and defiles many (Hebrews 12:15), and the word picture is exact: it grows down into you, spreads, and poisons more than the original wound ever did.

Unforgiveness is also corrosive to your relationship with God, because the same parable where the unforgiving servant is condemned is the one Jesus tells about us (Matthew 18:21-35). We who have been forgiven an unpayable debt cannot clutch the small debts owed to us without something going wrong in us. Holding it does not protect you. It deforms you.

## How to actually do it

Forgiveness is usually not a single moment but a decision you make and then keep remaking. Name the wrong specifically before God, the actual thing, not a vague haze. Say plainly what you are releasing: I forgive this person this debt, and I give up my right to repay them. Then, when the memory returns and the anger flares again, as it will, forgive again. Seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22) is not just about repeated offenses; it is also about the same offense you have to keep releasing as it keeps surfacing.

Pray for the person, which Jesus commands and which is nearly impossible at first and slowly becomes possible (Matthew 5:44). You cannot stay bitter toward someone you are genuinely asking God to bless. The prayer changes you long before it changes anything else, and changing you was always the point.

## This week

Name the specific wrong and the person who never apologized. Say out loud to God that you release the debt, that you give up the apology you are owed and the revenge you crave. When the bitterness rises again this week, do it again. Begin praying for that person, even badly, even reluctantly.

The apology may never come. Your freedom does not depend on it. Forgiveness is the one thing in this whole situation you can do without anyone's permission, and it is the thing that gets you out of the prison you did not choose.

title: How to Love a Difficult Family Member
excerpt: You cannot choose your family and you cannot fix them. But you can decide how you will love them, which is a different and more possible thing.
body:
Every family has one, and if you cannot think of who it is in yours, brace yourself, because it might be you. The difficult relative. The one whose call you hesitate to answer, whose name on the holiday list makes your stomach tighten, who has a gift for finding the soft spot and pressing it. You did not choose them and you cannot trade them, and the usual advice, just cut toxic people out of your life, runs into a wall when the toxic person is your mother or your brother or your grown child. So what do you actually do? You cannot fix them. You can decide how you will love them, and love, it turns out, is a verb you control even when the feelings will not cooperate.

## Love is a decision before it is a feeling

The culture treats love as something that happens to you, a feeling you either have or lack. The Bible treats love as something you do, a way of acting toward a person whether or not the warm feeling is present. When Jesus says love your enemies (Luke 6:27), he is obviously not commanding a feeling, because you cannot command a feeling. He is commanding action, do good to those who hate you, which you can in fact choose.

This reframes the whole problem. You are not failing because you do not feel affection for a difficult relative. You are asked to act lovingly toward them, to be patient, to refuse contempt, to seek their good, and that is a decision you can make on a day you feel nothing warm at all. Start there. The feeling, if it ever comes, comes later and is not the assignment.

## Accept the person you actually have

Most of the suffering with a difficult relative comes from fighting the reality of who they are. You keep expecting the apology they are never going to give, the change they are not going to make, the version of them you wish existed. Every holiday you walk in hoping this time will be different, and every time the hope is dashed, and the dashing is its own fresh wound.

There is a strange peace in accepting the person as they actually are rather than as you wish they were. This is not approval and it is not giving up; it is realism. When you stop expecting a critical person to suddenly become warm, their criticism still stings but it no longer shocks, and the shock was half the pain. Love them as they are, not as the corrected version you keep waiting for. You may be waiting your whole life for a person who is not coming.

## Set boundaries without slamming doors

Loving a difficult person does not mean absorbing endless harm. The most loving thing is sometimes a firm boundary, a limit on the access they have to wound you. You can love someone and still decide that you will leave when the conversation turns cruel, that you will not discuss certain topics, that the visit will be two hours and not two days. Even Jesus withdrew from people, and Proverbs is full of wisdom about distance from the contentious (Proverbs 22:24-25).

A boundary is not a punishment and it is not the opposite of love. It is what lets you keep loving without being destroyed, and what sometimes, over years, invites the other person to relate to you differently. The goal of the fence is not to wall them out forever. It is to make a relationship survivable, so that some love can keep flowing across it instead of the whole thing collapsing.

## Honor without obeying, and pray honestly

If the difficult person is a parent, the command to honor (Exodus 20:12) complicates everything, because people use it to demand that you submit to harm. But honor is not the same as obedience, and it is not the same as pretending the harm did not happen. You can honor a parent, speak respectfully of them, refuse to repay their cruelty in kind, care for their genuine needs, while still maintaining boundaries and not obeying unreasonable demands. Honor is a posture of respect, not a surrender of your safety or your adulthood.

And pray for them, honestly, which at first may mean telling God exactly how hard they are before you can ask anything good for them. It is difficult to stay hard toward someone you regularly carry to God. The prayer softens you, gives you patience you did not have, and occasionally, over a long time, becomes the channel through which something in them begins to change. But even if they never change, the praying changes you, and that was a gift God meant for you all along.

## This week

Name the difficult family member, and name the one expectation of them you keep clinging to that keeps getting crushed. Set it down; love the person who actually exists, not the one you wish for. Decide on one boundary that would make the relationship survivable, and begin praying for them, honestly, this week.

You cannot fix them and you cannot trade them. But love is a verb, and that one is yours to choose.
